answers.text: At our depot, every supplier email looks a little different, so I would tell the AI: always reply with exactly three lines, in this fixed order — delivery date, item and quantity, then any change from the original order, nothing else. That way whoever reads it gets a clear, tidy summary every time, no matter which email you feed in.

In my team, when we do the weekly expense claims, I would just say: list every claim under four columns — date, amount, category, submitter — in that order, one line per claim, so the memo always looks the same no matter who writes it.

Something is not quite right with the dates in this email — after a call on the 14th, saying the new date is the 19th but also 'three days out from today' does not really line up. I think the mix-up is in the dates rather than the price, since 100 times 48.50 comes to 4,850 anyway. I would not send it before someone looked at it again.

Looking at the numbers, 62 up from 54 checks out fine as around 15%. But 3 late out of 62 is not really 97% on time — that is closer to 95%, so that part looks off to me. I did not spot anything wrong with the stock line.

I would sign off Output 2, because it shows the actual sales and returns figures, not just the final percentage. Output 1 does not tell you what numbers it is based on, so there is nothing there to check against.

I would send Reply 2 as it stands, because it gives the order reference and the credit reference, so someone could look them up. Reply 1 sounds fine but you cannot tell if 'our error' and the 10% credit are actually true without a reference to check them against. That does not mean Reply 1 is wrong — once someone has confirmed the details behind it, it could go out too.
1. No, that is the customer's own address. 2. Yes, it is just a total, nothing about anyone. 3. No, that is not out yet. 4. Yes, it is already public. 5. No, that is personal.

I would be careful with the pricing and discount numbers, and the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies by name — I would leave those two out until someone has checked the tool is okay to use. The registration details and delivery schedule I am less sure about, so I would leave everything else out as well just to be safe.
I would add a step where, before the report goes out, I cross-check the total deliveries number against the depot log, and I would do that on the Friday before it is sent up, not after.

I think step 1, where the AI reads the order email, is the risky one because if it gets the quantity wrong everything after follows from that. But the real problem is step 4, sending the confirmation automatically — once that email is out, it is out, so that is where I would put a check before anything else.
